name: Per-ring zonal statistics with Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis

identity.method_name: Getis-Ord Gi* local spatial autocorrelation / hotspot statistic (PySAL esda.G_Local implementation; ArcGIS Pro 'Hot Spot Analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*)' equivalent), applied to a per-ring-sector encroachment index
identity.core_idea: For each lake, divide the legal buffer ring into angular sectors (or concentric sub-rings) and compute a per-sector encroachment index per year -- e.g. B3's building-intrusion count/overlap area, or a water/vegetation-loss magnitude. Gi* then tests, for each sector, whether its index value together with its spatially-defined neighbours' values is significantly higher (hot spot) or lower (cold spot) than expected under complete spatial randomness of that index across the fixed set of sectors, converting a bare per-sector number into a statistically-flagged claim of localised clustering rather than a raw pixel/footprint count.
identity.official_dataset_ids: Not a dataset; a statistical method. Depends on esda (PySAL, esda.G_Local, github.com/pysal/esda) and libpysal.weights for the spatial weights matrix; ArcGIS Pro equivalent tools are 'Hot Spot Analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*)' and 'Optimized Hot Spot Analysis'. Key comparison citation: Majd Mre, Bidyadhar Basa, Rabindro Nath Samal, 'Multi-season satellite analysis of surface water and vegetation dynamics in Chilika Lake from 2019 to 2025,' Discover Environment 4(1):364, Springer, published online 16 July 2026, doi 10.1007/s44274-026-00891-1.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Statistical test, not a label-substitution strategy: it does not create an encroachment label, it tests whether an already-computed encroachment-index value (from B3's building counts, or the water/vegetation classification) is spatially clustered beyond chance. It sits downstream of whichever proxy strategy produced the index and adds a significance layer on top, at no additional labelling cost -- only the statistical/software step (see student_days).
fit_to_project.input_required: A per-spatial-unit encroachment index (e.g. B3's building-intrusion count or overlap area per ring sector per lake-year) plus a spatial weights matrix defining sector adjacency (contiguity or k-nearest-neighbours). The project has neither yet: the ring/sector geometry and a per-sector index both depend on B1's buffer choice and B3's building-counting item being implemented first.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed, and this is the central caveat of the item. Gi* operates per spatial unit (ring sector), not per lake-year row. If a lake's ring is divided into 8-16 sectors and tested per lake-year, the effective n per single Gi* run is only 8-16 -- below the ~30-feature floor ArcGIS's own documentation states is needed for Optimized Hot Spot Analysis results to be considered reliable (https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/tool-reference/spatial-statistics/how-optimized-hot-spot-analysis-works.htm). Pooling one lake's sectors across all 7 years (e.g. 8 x 7 = 56) numerically clears 30 but is really only 8 distinct physical locations resampled repeatedly, a repeated-measures structure Gi* was not designed for; pooling across all 6 lakes into one 'global' run is not statistically coherent either, since the 6 lakes are spatially disjoint, not neighbours of each other. At this project's actual scale, per-lake-per-year Gi* does not meet the field's own reliability floor; the least-bad workable option is pooling one lake's sectors across years with the repeated-measures caveat disclosed.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes -- Gi* requires no encroachment labels, only index values and a spatial adjacency structure; it is a pure spatial-statistics test on whatever index is supplied.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Not directly applicable in the pixel sense -- Gi* operates on the ring/sector index values, whatever their source resolution. If the index comes from B3's building-footprint counting, resolution is set by that vector item, not the raster grid. If the index comes from the Sentinel-2 water/vegetation classifier, the 20 m grid limits how many independent sectors even a 30-75 m-wide ring can support: a thin ring subdivided into many angular sectors will contain very few, sometimes zero, independent 20 m pixels per sector, starving the index of signal before Gi* is even applied.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: none -- Gi* is an unsupervised spatial-statistics test, not a supervised method.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the four stated limitations directly -- it does not add rows, does not make OSM buildings multi-temporal, does not supply ground truth, and does not add imagery per year. Its value is orthogonal: it upgrades whatever per-ring index the project already computes (from B3 or the water/vegetation baseline) from a bare number into a statistically-qualified claim, which matters for defensibility rather than for any of the four named data limitations.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No -- Gi* tests spatial clustering of whatever index value it is given; it cannot tell whether a ring sector's high index value arose from desilting-driven water loss or genuine building encroachment. That discrimination must happen upstream, in how the index itself is constructed (e.g. using B3's building count rather than raw water-area change as Gi*'s input), not in the Gi* step.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No, for the same reason -- Gi* is agnostic to what produced its input index; if the index is derived from a water/vegetation classifier that already conflates hyacinth mats with terrestrial vegetation, Gi* will faithfully find 'hotspots' of that conflated signal. It adds no discriminating power over the hyacinth confound by itself.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: Indirect -- a statistically significant Gi* hotspot at a ring sector says 'this location's encroachment index is higher than chance given its neighbours,' which strengthens the case that a location merits attention, but it carries no legal weight of its own and does not map to a cadastral record; its evidentiary value is entirely inherited from whatever index and buffer distance (per B1) feed into it. Gi* significance is a claim about spatial pattern, not about legality -- a panel or court would still need the underlying building/footprint evidence (B3) and the chosen buffer's legal authority (B1); Gi* only says the pattern is unlikely to be random noise.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: The index fed into Gi* can vary year to year if it is B3's building-intrusion count (variable, given a genuinely multi-temporal footprint source) or the water/vegetation classification (already variable, one dry-season scene per year). Gi* itself is typically run separately per year (a static spatial test on that year's index snapshot), not as a spatiotemporal statistic; a proper space-time extension (e.g. an emerging hot spot analysis) is a distinct, more complex method not covered here and also not attempted by the Chilika Lake exemplar.

implementation.libraries: esda (PySAL: esda.G_Local, github.com/pysal/esda), libpysal (weights construction: Queen/Rook contiguity or k-nearest-neighbours via libpysal.weights), statsmodels (statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests, method='fdr_bh', for Benjamini-Hochberg correction, which is not built into esda), geopandas for building the ring-sector geometry and index table.
implementation.pretrained_weights: not applicable -- Gi* is a closed-form/permutation-based statistic, not a trained model.
implementation.licence: esda and libpysal are BSD-3-Clause (PySAL project), unrestricted for academic use. ArcGIS Pro's Hot Spot Analysis tool requires a licensed ArcGIS Pro seat (Esri commercial licence) if used instead of PySAL/esda; the free PySAL/esda route is the correct choice given this project's budget and compute constraints.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial, CPU-only -- Gi* on a few dozen spatial units with 999 permutations (PySAL's default) runs in well under a second on a laptop; no GPU, no Colab/Kaggle allocation is needed for this item at all.
implementation.student_days: 1-1.5 student-days: constructing the ring-sector geometry and its adjacency/weights matrix, including correct 360-degree wrap-around handling (0.5 day); running esda.G_Local with star=True and 999 permutations per lake-year (0.25 day); and applying pooled Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across all lake-year-sector tests plus writing up the small-n caveat honestly (0.25-0.5 day).

evaluation.metrics: Gi* z-scores and permutation-based pseudo p-values (p_sim, preferred over the analytic normal-theory p-value given small n and non-normal index distributions) per ring sector per lake-year, reported only after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the full pooled set of tests -- not per-sector uncorrected p<0.05, which inflates apparent significance.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Not a predictive train/test method, so no lake/year hold-out split applies in the usual ML sense. The correct protocol is a pre-registered spatial-weights and correction scheme: fix the sector-adjacency definition, the permutation count (999), and the FDR procedure before inspecting which sectors come out significant, and apply FDR correction across the entire pooled set of tests run (all sectors x all lake-years), not per lake or per year separately, to avoid inflating the count of 'significant' hotspots reported.
evaluation.leakage_risk: The dominant risk is not train/test leakage but multiple-comparison inflation: this project's design plausibly runs on the order of 300+ individual Gi* tests (e.g. 8 sectors x 6 lakes x 7 years = 336), at which uncorrected alpha=0.05 would flag roughly 16-17 'significant' hotspots by chance alone even with zero true clustering -- these false hotspots look exactly like real encroachment findings unless FDR correction is applied to the pooled p-value set. A secondary risk is treating repeated-measures pooling (the same 8 sectors resampled across 7 years) as 56 independent spatial units, when it is really only 8 independent physical locations -- this must be disclosed, not used to silently claim the n=30 reliability floor is met when it is not really met independently.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: Gi* natively reports a permutation-based pseudo p-value (p_sim) as its uncertainty measure, more defensible than a bare point z-score alone, but this project must additionally disclose the small-n floor problem (n=8-16 sectors per lake-year vs the ~30-unit floor ArcGIS's own documentation states is needed for reliable Optimized Hot Spot Analysis results) as a stated limitation on top of the p-value itself, since the p-value's face-value validity is questionable below that floor regardless of how it is computed.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: not applicable -- no synthetic data generation or augmentation is involved in a Gi* run on an already-computed index.

evidence.published_performance: Not a predictive-accuracy method, so no accuracy/F1-style number applies. The closest evidence is methodological: ArcGIS's own documentation states Hot Spot Analysis / Optimized Hot Spot Analysis results 'aren't reliable when there are less than 30 features' (https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/tool-reference/spatial-statistics/how-optimized-hot-spot-analysis-works.htm), and ArcGIS Online's Find Hot Spots additionally requires >=60 points and >=30 nonempty aggregation cells (https://doc.arcgis.com/en/arcgis-online/analyze/find-hot-spots-mv.htm) -- practitioner rules of thumb from Esri's own tool documentation, not a theorem from the original Getis and Ord (1992, Geographical Analysis 24:189-206) or Ord and Getis (1995, doi 10.1111/j.1538-4632.1995.tb00912.x) papers.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: The n>=30 floor guidance comes from Esri's general-purpose ArcGIS Pro/Online documentation, not from any lake- or India-specific study, so it is a generic statistical-reliability threshold, not a study-specific forecast. The Chilika Lake exemplar (doi 10.1007/s44274-026-00891-1) ran Gi* at a completely different scale: individual 10 m x 10 m Sentinel-2 pixels (100 m^2) reclassified into a 5-class encroachment scheme and converted to points, with k=8 nearest-neighbour weights. [uncertain] The paper does not state one explicit sample-size number for the Gi* input point set, but it is implicitly very large -- Chilika's dry-season water area alone spans 693-748 km^2 across the study years (the paper's own Table 2), so at 100 m^2/pixel the underlying pixel population is in the millions and the 'moderate/strong encroachment' point subset almost certainly numbers in the thousands to tens of thousands -- 2-3+ orders of magnitude larger than the 8-16 sectors per lake this project could realistically construct.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: Yes, via the Chilika Lake exemplar specifically: Majd Mre, Bidyadhar Basa, Rabindro Nath Samal, 'Multi-season satellite analysis of surface water and vegetation dynamics in Chilika Lake from 2019 to 2025,' Discover Environment 4(1):364 (2026), doi 10.1007/s44274-026-00891-1 -- confirmed as a real, open-access (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) paper pairing Gi* with multi-season NDWI (threshold >=0.05) / NDVI (threshold >=0.30, nearly identical to this project's own NDVI>0.30 baseline) differencing across 2019/2021/2023/2025 wet- and dry-season Sentinel-2 composites, for India's largest lagoon. It is methodologically analogous in spirit (same statistic, same sensor, near-identical NDVI threshold, similar year range) but NOT analogous in spatial-unit design: Chilika runs Gi* on a dense pixel/point cloud with k=8 nearest-neighbour weights, not coarse ring/sector zonal units. Notably, the paper's full text contains no mention of 'false discovery,' 'FDR,' 'Bonferroni,' or 'multiple compar[ison]' anywhere -- it applies no multiple-testing correction to its own Gi* output, despite separately (in an unrelated Pearson-correlation section of the same paper) cautioning that strong spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I 0.45-0.76) can make 'conventional p-values ... overestimate statistical significance.' No other 2020+ Getis-Ord Gi* study on Indian lakes or wetlands addressing encroachment was found; Chilika 2026 appears to be the only close Indian-lake analogue currently in the literature.
evidence.evidence_recency: 2026 for the Chilika Lake exemplar (published online 16 July 2026, Discover Environment, Springer) -- the strongest and most directly relevant evidence is current at the time of this research. Foundational statistic papers, Getis and Ord 1992 (Geographical Analysis 24:189-206) and Ord and Getis 1995 (doi 10.1111/j.1538-4632.1995.tb00912.x), are pre-2000 but are the original methodological source, not the applied evidence base; ArcGIS's small-n guidance is from currently-maintained (2024-2026) Esri Pro documentation. Nothing load-bearing for the applied evidence is pre-2020.
evidence.primary_sources: Chilika Lake paper: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-026-00891-1 (doi 10.1007/s44274-026-00891-1); Getis and Ord 1992 original G statistic, Geographical Analysis 24:189-206; Ord and Getis 1995 Gi* extension: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1538-4632.1995.tb00912.x (doi 10.1111/j.1538-4632.1995.tb00912.x); esda documentation: https://pysal.org/esda/generated/esda.G_Local.html and https://github.com/pysal/esda; ArcGIS Pro Hot Spot Analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*): https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/tool-reference/spatial-statistics/hot-spot-analysis.htm and https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/tool-reference/spatial-statistics/h-how-hot-spot-analysis-getis-ord-gi-spatial-stati.htm; Optimized Hot Spot Analysis reliability floor: https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/tool-reference/spatial-statistics/how-optimized-hot-spot-analysis-works.htm; ArcGIS Online Find Hot Spots minimum-feature requirement: https://doc.arcgis.com/en/arcgis-online/analyze/find-hot-spots-mv.htm; statsmodels FDR correction: https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests.html; GPS/IoT geofencing sense confirmed as a distinct domain via ArcGIS Velocity's Geofence analysis tool: https://doc.arcgis.com/en/velocity/analyze/geofencing-analysis.htm, and industry glossary sources https://www.samsara.com/guides/geofencing and https://www.verizonconnect.com/glossary/what-is-a-geofence/.

risk.failure_modes: (1) Running Gi* per-lake-per-year on 8-16 ring sectors, well under the ~30-feature reliability floor stated in ArcGIS's own Optimized Hot Spot Analysis documentation, and reporting the resulting p-values as if they were as trustworthy as a properly-powered spatial analysis. (2) Running 300+ pooled sector-year tests (e.g. 8 sectors x 6 lakes x 7 years = 336) and reporting uncorrected p<0.05 hits as 'significant hotspots,' when roughly 16-17 such hits are expected by chance alone at that scale with zero true clustering -- Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the pooled set is mandatory, not optional, and the closest published analogue (Chilika Lake, doi 10.1007/s44274-026-00891-1) itself applies no such correction, so it cannot be cited as a precedent for skipping this step. (3) Pooling one lake's sectors across all 7 years to numerically clear the n=30 floor while treating the result as 56 independent units, when it is really a repeated-measures resampling of only 8 physical locations -- a structure ordinary Gi* was not designed for. (4) Treating a Gi* hotspot as evidence of encroachment causation or of illegality, when it only establishes that the input index is spatially clustered beyond chance -- it says nothing about what caused the clustering (desilting, hyacinth misclassification, or genuine building intrusion), which must be established by the upstream index construction (B3), not by Gi* itself.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask 'do you have enough spatial units for this statistic to mean anything?' and 'did you correct for testing hundreds of ring segments at once?' This item survives only if both are answered honestly: state the actual per-lake-per-year sector count (8-16, below Esri's own 30-unit floor), state the total number of pooled tests run and the FDR correction applied to that full pooled set, and explicitly disclose that even the closest published methodological analogue (Chilika, 2026) operates at a spatial-unit density 2-3 orders of magnitude finer (pixel/point-level with k=8 nearest-neighbour weights) than anything a 6-lake, ring-sector project can achieve, and itself omits FDR correction -- so it can justify the general Gi*-plus-NDWI/NDVI-differencing pipeline concept, but not skipping FDR correction here.
risk.honest_expectation: At this project's actual scale (6 lakes, single-digit-to-low-double-digit ring sectors per lake, 7 years), Gi* run per-lake-per-year does not meet the field's own stated reliability floor for meaningful inference. The realistic, defensible outcome is either (a) not to run per-lake-per-year Gi* at all and instead report simple ranked/sorted sector index values with the small-n caveat stated plainly, or (b) run Gi* on sectors pooled across all 7 years within each lake (n=56, really 8 independent locations resampled), report it as an exploratory, FDR-corrected, repeated-measures-caveated result rather than a confirmed hotspot map, and be explicit that this falls well short of the pixel/point-level density the closest published Indian-lake analogue actually used. A null or 'not statistically meaningful at this scale' finding for some or most lakes is a plausible, honest, and reportable outcome, not a failure of the analysis.

verdict.recommended_rank: consider-with-reasons -- the statistic itself is cheap (1-1.5 student-days, CPU-only, free BSD-licensed PySAL) and would meaningfully upgrade a bare per-ring index into a disclosed, FDR-corrected significance claim, but the project's actual ring-sector count (8-16 per lake) sits below the field's own ~30-unit reliability floor, so it should be presented as an exploratory add-on with that limitation stated up front, not as the project's headline statistical result.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: Getis-Ord Gi* (via PySAL's esda.G_Local, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across all pooled ring-sector tests) can flag which parts of a lake's buffer ring show statistically unusual clustering of an encroachment index, closely following the 2025-26 Chilika Lake Sentinel-2 precedent (doi 10.1007/s44274-026-00891-1), but with only 8-16 ring sectors per lake this project falls below the ~30-spatial-unit floor the statistic's own documentation says is needed for reliable results, so any hotspot claim must be reported as exploratory, not confirmatory; and for the viva, this project's 'geo-fencing' means a static legal buffer polygon tested against satellite/vector evidence over multiple years, not the GPS/IoT real-time device-alert sense of the term, which plays no role here.
